reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Occurs through the scar of a previous abdominal wound where the fascial closure has failed, presenting as a bulge that enlarges with straining
Risk factors include wound infection, obesity, poor surgical technique, emergency surgery, chronic cough, steroids, diabetes, malnutrition, and smoking
The defect and sac often enlarge over time, and large long-standing hernias may develop multiple loculations and adhesions
Small defects with a narrow neck carry a higher risk of incarceration and strangulation than broad-necked defects
Very large hernias may result in loss of abdominal domain, where returning contents to the abdomen risks respiratory compromise and abdominal compartment syndrome
Repair is usually with mesh, either open (onlay, sublay/retrorectus, or intraperitoneal) or laparoscopic, as suture-only repair of larger defects has high recurrence
Optimising modifiable risk factors such as weight, glycaemic control, and smoking before elective repair improves outcomes
A previous wound dehiscence or a burst abdomen strongly predisposes to later incisional herniation
reference.pathophysiology: An incisional hernia develops when the musculo-aponeurotic layers of a healed surgical wound fail to maintain their integrity, allowing peritoneum and abdominal contents to protrude beneath the intact skin. Impaired wound healing, whether from infection, ischaemia, raised intra-abdominal pressure, technical factors, or patient factors such as obesity, diabetes, and malnutrition, weakens the fascial repair. Over time the defect enlarges and the sac expands, sometimes housing much of the abdominal contents. Narrow-necked defects can trap and strangulate bowel, while very large defects lead to loss of domain and altered abdominal wall mechanics.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent primary ventral hernia at another site
Seroma or haematoma at the operative site
Desmoid or other abdominal wall tumour
Intra-abdominal mass bulging through a weak scar
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the scar, defect size, and reducibility
CT abdomen and pelvis to define defect size, contents, and loss of domain and to plan repair
Ultrasound for smaller or uncertain defects
Assessment and optimisation of comorbidities before elective repair
redFlags: Irreducible, tender bulge with loss of cough impulse indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency)
Bowel obstruction associated with the hernia
Skin breakdown or ischaemia over a large or rapidly enlarging hernia
Systemic sepsis or peritonism from strangulated bowel
reference.prognosis: Recurrence rates are higher than for primary hernias but are substantially reduced by mesh repair and by optimising risk factors. Large hernias with loss of domain require specialised techniques and carry greater perioperative risk, while emergency presentation with strangulation increases morbidity.
pitfalls: Performing suture-only repair of a sizeable defect and accepting a high recurrence risk
Failing to optimise obesity, diabetes, and smoking before elective repair
Underestimating loss of domain and precipitating abdominal compartment syndrome at repair
Overlooking a small tender defect that is at high risk of strangulation
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Preoperative optimisation of modifiable risk factors including weight reduction, glycaemic control and smoking cessation before elective repair
Mesh reinforcement as the standard repair, whether open retrorectus/sublay or laparoscopic, since suture-only repair of larger defects recurs frequently
Component separation techniques and abdominal wall reconstruction for large defects with loss of domain, sometimes aided by preoperative botulinum toxin or progressive pneumoperitoneum
Emergency surgical repair for incarceration or strangulation, particularly with narrow-necked defects
Conservative management with an abdominal support garment for small asymptomatic hernias or patients unfit for surgery
Cross-sectional imaging to plan repair and structured follow-up for recurrence within a specialist abdominal wall service
